title: Princeton PhD Student Eva Yi Xie Detained by ICE After Neuroscience Conference
excerpt: Her lawyers say a pending asylum claim lets her stay; ICE says she never had authorisation to study in the US. A federal judge has barred her removal from Virginia while her habeas petition is heard.
body:
• Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Princeton neuroscience PhD student, was detained by ICE at Reagan National Airport on Thursday, November 19, after presenting at a conference in Washington, D.C.
  • Her lawyer says her original nonimmigrant status has expired but she has a pending asylum application and an immigration court hearing set for early 2028; ICE says she never had authorisation to study in the US and was admitted temporarily in March 2016 with a required departure date of September 15, 2016.
  • A federal judge on Friday blocked ICE from removing her from the Eastern District of Virginia and ordered the government to respond to her habeas petition by 5 p.m. on Wednesday, November 25.
  • Princeton has arranged legal counsel for Xie, who is being held at a facility in Chantilly, Virginia.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year doctoral student in neuroscience at Princeton University, was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Reagan National Airport on Thursday, November 19, as she travelled home from the Society for Neuroscience annual meeting in Washington, D.C., where she had presented her research. She is being held at an ICE facility in Chantilly, Virginia, according to Princeton Alumni Weekly.

Two accounts of her status

Xie's lawyer, Kerry Doyle, told The Daily Princetonian that Xie is an asylum seeker with an immigration court date set for early 2028, and her lawyers argue her pending asylum application allows her to remain in the country. ICE gave a different account in a statement to Newsweek late Friday: the agency said Xie never had authorisation to study in the United States, that she was granted temporary admission in March 2016 with a required departure date of September 15, 2016, and that a pending application would not confer legal status. ICE said the airport arrest was a targeted enforcement operation and that she will be detained until her hearing, receiving due process. Which account prevails is now a question for the courts, not for either side's statements.

The court steps, and the dates that matter

Xie's lawyers have filed a habeas corpus petition in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, alleging she is being held illegally. Late Friday, District Judge Anthony J. Trenga ordered that Xie not be removed from the judicial district without further direction from the court, and required immigration officials to respond to the petition by 5 p.m. on Wednesday, November 25. Her underlying immigration court hearing is scheduled for early 2028, according to her lawyer.

Who Xie is

Xie emigrated to the US from China in 2016 and attended the Bronx High School of Science, where she was a Regeneron Science Talent Search finalist. She graduated from MIT in 2024 with a double major in AI and Decision Making and in Mathematics, and worked in Professor Ila Fiete's lab as an undergraduate. At Princeton, in Professor Carlos Brody's lab, her research uses mouse experiments and large neural recording datasets to study how brain regions work together in decision-making, according to STAT's reporting. At last year's NeurIPS conference she convened a workshop bringing together AI and neuroscience researchers.

"Eva is a brilliant law-abiding student and wonderful person who has many talents to contribute to the United States. Detaining her, with the intent of deporting her, makes no sense whatsoever."

— Carlos Brody, Xie's PhD adviser, to The Daily Princetonian

The university's response, and the wider chill

Princeton spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss said the university has arranged legal counsel to represent Xie. Graduate School Dean Rodney D. Priestley said the news was distressing for the Princeton community and that the university hopes she will soon be able to resume her studies. The detention has travelled quickly through academic circles: MIT's The Tech reported it as the first case of ICE detaining an MIT graduate or student, and STAT reported that a report released this week found international graduate student enrolment down by a third at academic medical centres.

What this means for international students

Xie's case turns on her individual status — a pending asylum claim, not a student visa — and readers should not read it as a change in the rules for F-1 students. The practical lesson her colleagues are drawing is narrower: domestic air travel, not just international travel, is where her detention happened, and travellers whose status involves any pending application or expired document should confirm their position with an immigration lawyer before flying. The next concrete development is the government's response to the habeas petition, due November 25. Our coverage of another recent detention, the Bronx food pantry founder held after a court hearing, shows how differently these cases can proceed.
